analysis.one_liner: Bars debt buyers from suing poor countries for more than they paid for the countries' defaulted debt.
analysis.headline: A bill to stop 'vulture' funds from suing heavily indebted poor countries for big profits on cheaply bought debt was introduced by Rep. Maxine Waters with 9 cosponsors and died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful for investors ('vulture creditors') to buy the defaulted debt of very poor countries cheaply and then sue to collect far more than they paid, capping their recovery at the purchase price plus 6% simple interest a year. It would also bar U.S. courts from issuing any judgment or seizure order that furthers such a claim, and require collectors of a poor country's debt to disclose under oath who owns the claim and what they paid for it, with those affidavits filed as public records at the Treasury Department.
analysis.who_benefits: Citizens of the world's most heavily indebted poor countries, whose debt relief and aid money would stay in the country instead of being diverted to litigation by speculators, and the taxpayers of donor countries who fund that debt relief.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any U.S.-connected person to seek payment on a poor country's defaulted debt in excess of what they paid for it plus 6% simple interest per year, with violators fined the full amount they sought.

Bars U.S. courts from issuing summonses, judgments, attachments, or executions in aid of a claim that would further sovereign debt profiteering, and voids any such process issued in violation of the bill.

Requires anyone seeking to collect a poor country's sovereign debt in U.S. courts to file sworn affidavits disclosing all owners of the claim, the purchase price, and the date of purchase, and requires those affidavits be kept as public records at Treasury, so the true holders of the debt can no longer hide behind offshore entities.

Requires Treasury to notify the affected countries of the law's protections and report annually to Congress on how the law has supported the international Heavily Indebted Poor Countries debt relief initiative.

analysis.who_pays: Investors and hedge funds that buy defaulted sovereign debt at a discount and profit by suing poor countries for full face value, plus other creditors in that market who would face a cap on recoveries.

drawbacks.text: Capping recovery at purchase price plus 6% would sharply reduce any incentive to buy a poor country's defaulted debt at all, which could shrink the market for distressed sovereign debt and raise the cost for poor countries to borrow or restructure their debts.

The bill would apply to court actions already pending when it took effect, canceling remedies investors believed they had under their debt contracts, and imposes a penalty equal to the entire amount a collector sought — an unusually harsh remedy that critics would call an unfair retroactive taking.

The definition of a vulture creditor sweeps in any buyer of defaulted sovereign debt at a discount, not just aggressive hold-out litigants, so even ordinary creditors who took a loss on a loan and bought others' debt could be barred from recovering more than they paid.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real, documented harm: speculators buying a poor country's debt for pennies and suing for full value, which the bill's own findings say siphons debt relief meant for the poorest citizens and disrupts U.S. foreign relations. The remedy, however, is blunt — a 6%-interest cap and penalties for all discounted buyers would likely dry up most secondary-market purchases of distressed poor-country debt, and that lost liquidity is a genuine cost to the same countries the bill aims to help. A narrower bill targeting hold-out litigation specifically would have handled the tradeoff more carefully.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary and Financial Services committees in August 2008, and neither committee took it up before that Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxine Waters introduced the Stop VULTURE Funds Act on August 1, 2008, joined by seven other members as original sponsors.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the House Financial Services Committee.
The bill attracted 9 cosponsors, all Democrats.
No further action appears in the bill's record: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action, before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Vulture funds and distressed-debt investors are better off, because the legal cap on their collections was never enacted and U.S. courts remained open to suits against poor countries. Nothing in the record shows organized opposition; the bill simply received no committee action in the two months remaining in the session.

for.name: Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop VULTURE Funds Act and wrote its findings documenting how vulture creditors siphon debt relief from poor countries.

for.name: 9 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a 10-member sponsoring bloc.

against.name: House Judiciary and Financial Services Committees
against.role: Committees to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Barney Frank
against.what_they_did: Chaired one of the two committees the bill was referred to; the committee never considered it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, but no member or group is recorded as opposing it; the bill died without any vote, so the partisan shape of the opposition was never tested.

industries.industry: Vulture funds and distressed sovereign debt investors
industries.note: The bill outlaws their core business model — buying a poor country's defaulted debt cheaply and suing for far more — and caps recovery at purchase price plus 6%. The bill's findings describe their collections as diverting aid and debt relief meant for poor countries' citizens.

The bill targets funds that operate through offshore shells despite being U.S.-owned, by making any person U.S.-controlled or acting on U.S. soil subject to the prohibition and requiring full disclosure of claim ownership.
A recovery cap would shrink the market for defaulted poor-country debt, cutting both speculative profits and the liquidity that lets distressed creditors sell their claims at a loss.

industries.industry: Official and multilateral creditors (IMF, World Bank, African Development Fund)
industries.note: The bill's findings say preferential payments to hold-out funds come at the expense of these creditors and of the $50 billion-plus in international debt relief they and donor governments have committed, so the cap would protect those relief programs.
